title: Peri-operative diabetes, SGLT2 inhibitors and steroid cover
subtitle: Keep glucose safe, avoid ketoacidosis, prevent adrenal crisis

sources.org: Centre for Perioperative Care (CPOC) with the Joint British Diabetes Societies for Inpatient Care (JBDS-IP)
sources.title: Guideline for perioperative care for people with diabetes mellitus undergoing elective and emergency surgery

sources.org: Association of Anaesthetists, Royal College of Physicians and Society for Endocrinology
sources.title: Guidelines for the management of glucocorticoids during the peri-operative period for patients with adrenal insufficiency

sources.org: American Heart Association and American College of Cardiology (AHA/ACC)
sources.title: 2024 AHA/ACC guideline for perioperative cardiovascular management for noncardiac surgery

red_flags.text: Nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, tachypnoea or acidosis in a patient on an SGLT2 inhibitor, even with a normal glucose: euglycaemic diabetic ketoacidosis. Check blood ketones.
Unexplained hypotension, hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia or hypoglycaemia in a patient on long-term steroids or with known adrenal insufficiency: adrenal crisis.
Type 1 diabetes: never omit basal insulin, even when fasting. Omission causes ketoacidosis within hours.
Capillary glucose below 4 mmol/L or persistently above 12 mmol/L around surgery.
HbA1c above 69 mmol/mol (8.5%) before elective surgery.

do_now.text: Check HbA1c from the last three months at pre-assessment; if above 69 mmol/mol (8.5%), refer for optimisation and consider deferring elective surgery.
Place people with diabetes early on the operating list to minimise fasting.
Target capillary glucose of 6 to 10 mmol/L, accepting 4 to 12 mmol/L, and check at least hourly during surgery.

SGLT2 inhibitors: stop 3 days before elective surgery (4 days for ertugliflozin), per the 2024 AHA/ACC guideline and product labelling. Some UK guidance uses a shorter omission; follow the local policy and document the plan.

Steroid cover for adrenal insufficiency or long-term glucocorticoids: give hydrocortisone 100 mg intravenously at induction for surgery under general or regional anaesthesia, then continued cover per the 2020 guideline.

assess.text: Type of diabetes, every glucose-lowering drug and its timing, hypoglycaemia awareness, and complications: renal, cardiac, autonomic neuropathy.
Steroid exposure: dose, duration and when stopped. Convert to prednisolone equivalent to compare preparations.
How many meals will be missed. One missed meal is often managed by adjusting medication; more than one, or poor control, usually needs a variable rate intravenous insulin infusion.
Renal function for metformin and other agents.

investigate.text: Capillary glucose on admission and hourly during surgery and recovery.
Blood ketones in anyone on an SGLT2 inhibitor who is unwell, and routinely before surgery in many local protocols.
Electrolytes, including potassium, during an insulin infusion.
Venous gas for acidosis if ketones are raised or the patient is unwell.

resuscitate.text: Reduce long-acting basal insulin by 20% on the evening before and the day of surgery; continue it alongside any intravenous insulin infusion.
Use a variable rate intravenous insulin infusion with glucose-containing fluid when more than one meal will be missed, when control is poor, or in emergency surgery with hyperglycaemia.
Adjust oral agents according to the CPOC drug table, which specifies the day before and the day of surgery for each class.
Ketones raised in a patient on an SGLT2 inhibitor: treat as diabetic ketoacidosis with glucose and insulin even if blood glucose is normal, and involve the diabetes team.

Steroids, major surgery: after the induction dose, continue hydrocortisone by infusion (200 mg over 24 hours) or 50 mg 6-hourly by injection until oral intake resumes, then double the usual oral dose for 48 hours or longer after complicated surgery.

definitive.text: Restart usual diabetes medication once eating and drinking; overlap the subcutaneous insulin with the infusion before stopping it, typically with a meal.
Restart SGLT2 inhibitors only when the patient is eating and drinking normally and is clinically well.
Steroid cover is not needed beyond the usual dose for minor procedures under local anaesthesia; for intermediate and major surgery follow the graded 2020 guideline schedule.
Suspected adrenal crisis: hydrocortisone 100 mg intravenously immediately, intravenous fluids, and then continued hydrocortisone; do not delay for a cortisol result.
Discharge with a written plan for diabetes medication and, for steroid-dependent patients, sick-day rules and a steroid emergency card.

escalate.text: Inpatient diabetes team for type 1 diabetes, insulin pumps, poor control, ketosis or recurrent hypoglycaemia.
Endocrinology for uncertain adrenal status or complex steroid regimens.
Critical care for diabetic ketoacidosis, hyperosmolar state or adrenal crisis with shock.

notes: Euglycaemic ketoacidosis is the trap: an SGLT2 inhibitor keeps the glucose normal while the patient becomes acidotic. Check ketones, not just glucose.
Steroid cover is cheap and adrenal crisis is lethal. When steroid exposure is uncertain, give the cover.
Most peri-operative diabetes harm comes from omitted basal insulin in type 1 diabetes and prolonged fasting, both of which are preventable at pre-assessment.
